new_statements.quote: Stress is marked with [´] on the vowel, or first vowel of a group except where evidence suggests that the second vowel is to be stressed. I have not marked stress on phonemicised forms of French words, since it is not possible to reconstruct this. In transcriptions of Spanish forms, I have followed Spanish stress rules. Stress in Gatschet's material is irregular, there being no one syllable which customarily receives stress, and thus is probably the best source of evidence about stress placement in Karankawa. [...] The provisional phonemic inventory of Karankawa might be posited as: /p t ts č k kw b d g s š x kl gl l w j m n h '/ for consonants, /i e a o u ii ee aa oo uu/ for vowels, and free stress, with a syllabic canon of (C) V(:) (C) (C).

new_statements.rule_in_words: No fixed stress position can be established: in the only accent-marked corpus (Gatschet 1891) stress falls on no one customary syllable, so Grant provisionally posits free (lexical) stress. Gatschet himself (1891: 89/153) observed that the radical syllable is often the accented one, with the accent moving to the final syllable when the termination is stressed or long (ámel ~ amé-el, kóta ~ kotá).
new_statements.exceptions: Grant marks stress only from Gatschet's records; Spanish-matrix (Chowell) forms are given Spanish stress by convention and French-matrix forms are left unmarked, so they carry no evidence. Gatschet notes accent doublets (ámel/amé-el, kóta/kotá) and penult stress on Spanish loans. Grant flags the whole phonology as 'extremely tentative'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms from an extinct language recorded in 1884-1889 from non-native rememberers (Alice W. Oliver; two Tonkawa speakers); Grant warns Gatschet 'was not working with native speakers, and phonological cruces should not stand or fall on his evidence alone'.
new_statements.identity_note: Karankawa (kara1289, ISO zkk), extinct isolate of the Texas Gulf coast. All stress evidence comes from Gatschet's 1884-1889 records (chiefly Alice W. Oliver's remembered vocabulary from Matagorda Bay, plus a few words from two Tonkawa), i.e. one late variety filtered through non-native speakers; Grant stresses high internal dialectal diversity across the 1689-1889 sources.

sources.note: Introduction only says 'The accents in Comecrudo, Cotoname, and the Karankawa recorded by Dr. Gatschet are as given by the last named investigator'; vocabulary with accent marks, no stress-system statement.

sources.citation: Gatschet, Albert S. 1891. The Karankawa Indians, the coast people of Texas. Archaeological and Ethnological Papers of the Peabody Museum, Harvard University, 1(2). Cambridge, MA.
sources.note: p. 89 (=153 in volume pagination; PDF p. 98), paragraph 'Accentuation': 'In many words of the vocabularies the radical syllable is the accented one, and when stress is laid upon the termination, or when the terminal becomes long in quantity, the accent advances to the ultimate syllable: ámel and amé-el, kóta and kotá. The few Spanish words of the vocabularies are emphasized upon the penult...' (Earlier scan note that Gatschet had no system statement was wrong.) Data from non-native rememberers (Mrs Oliver, two Tonkawa).
